npcsInvolved.name: The Queen of Hearts
npcsInvolved.description: Tall, regal, and terrifying, the Queen of Hearts is a force of nature wearing a crown. Her rage is legendary, her cruelty is systematic, and her power over Wonderland is near-absolute — when she decrees something, reality bends to accommodate. She rules through fear, enforced by her Vorpal Guard and an army of card-soldiers who are more afraid of her than of any enemy. She is vain, volatile, and utterly convinced of her own infallibility. But beneath the tyranny, she is also a victim — the Crown of Hearts has been corrupting her for centuries, amplifying her worst traits and suppressing her empathy until the original fey noble she once was is buried under layers of cruelty and paranoia. Defeating her is necessary; pitying her is optional but adds depth.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The Queen wants absolute control. She wants to be feared, obeyed, and adored (in that order). She destroyed the Looking Glass because it represented a connection to the outside world that she could not control — if people could leave Wonderland, they could escape her rule. She keeps the seventh shard in her crown because its power amplifies her own. She will fight to the death to maintain her authority, not because she loves power for its own sake, but because the Crown of Hearts has made her incapable of imagining life without it.

npcsInvolved.name: The King of Hearts
npcsInvolved.description: A small, round, anxious man who is the physical and temperamental opposite of his wife. The King of Hearts sweats constantly, speaks in a perpetual nervous mutter, and has spent centuries trying to make himself as small and unnoticeable as possible. He is genuinely kind, secretly brave, and has been undermining the Queen in tiny ways for decades — mislaying execution orders, pardoning prisoners, hiding the Vorpal Sword in his throne for the day someone brave enough to use it arrives. He is the Queen's greatest vulnerability because he is the only person in the palace she has not completely terrorized — she loves him, in her twisted way, and this sliver of genuine emotion is the crack in her armor.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The King wants Wonderland to be free and his wife to be saved — though he knows these goals may be incompatible. He has been waiting for heroes capable of challenging the Queen, hoarding the Vorpal Sword and gathering intelligence for decades. His moment of courage — standing up to the Queen in the Throne Room — is something he has imagined a thousand times but never had the bravery to attempt. The party gives him that bravery.

npcsInvolved.name: The Knave of Hearts
npcsInvolved.description: A young, handsome card-knight with a face that suggests both nobility and mischief. The Knave of Hearts was the Queen's favorite courtier until he made the mistake of not laughing at one of her jokes. She framed him for stealing tarts (which she ate herself) and now he faces execution for a crime that never happened. Despite his dire situation, the Knave maintains a sardonic wit and quiet dignity that makes him instantly likeable. He is also a skilled fighter — before his arrest, he was the captain of the palace guard.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The Knave wants to survive, clear his name, and see justice done. He does not seek vengeance against the Queen — he pities her, which is perhaps the most insulting thing anyone has ever felt toward her. He will fight alongside the party with skill and loyalty if freed, and his knowledge of the palace layout is invaluable.

npcsInvolved.name: The Card Painters (2, 5, and 7 of Spades)
npcsInvolved.description: Three low-ranking card-soldiers assigned to the most humiliating duty in the palace: painting white roses red, every single day, knowing the paint will wash off in the next rain. The 2 of Spades is a veteran rebel who has been planning an uprising for years, gathering supplies and intelligence with painstaking care. The 5 of Spades is an emotional wreck who cries at the drop of a hat but is fiercely loyal to her friends. The 7 of Spades is a cheerful pragmatist who paints with genuine artistry and treats each day as an adventure, refusing to let the Queen's tyranny crush his spirit.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The painters want freedom — from the painting duty, from the Queen's arbitrary cruelty, and from the constant fear of execution. The 2 of Spades sees the party as the catalyst her rebellion has been waiting for. The 5 of Spades just wants to stop being afraid. The 7 of Spades wants to paint something other than roses for once in his life.

rewards.story: The party has overthrown the Queen of Hearts and freed Wonderland from tyranny. The Looking Glass is restored, creating a permanent gateway between Wonderland and the material plane. The King of Hearts — the legitimate ruler — begins the slow process of rebuilding a realm shattered by centuries of cruelty. The card-soldiers lay down their arms. The painters put away their red paint. And somewhere in the Tea Quarter, a clock ticks steadily past six, the Hatter hosts a real tea party, and the March Hare introduces his children to the heroes who saved their world. Wonderland will never be normal — it was never meant to be — but it can be wonderful again. The party's choices throughout the campaign determined how this ending unfolds: a Wonderland fully free and rebuilding, a Wonderland partially free but still scarred, or a Wonderland escaped but left to its fate. Every ally earned, every NPC helped, every act of kindness rippled outward to shape this final moment. The adventure in Wonderland is over. The wonder is just beginning.

twists: The Queen of Hearts is not purely evil — the Crown of Hearts has been corrupting her for centuries, amplifying her worst traits and suppressing her empathy. Removing the crown reveals a confused, frightened fey noble who barely remembers the person she used to be. This does not absolve her of responsibility, but it adds moral complexity to her defeat.

The Vorpal Guard's weapons are bonded to the Crown of Hearts — destroying the crown to free the Queen also destroys the vorpal enchantments on their axes. The only independent vorpal weapon is the Vorpal Sword hidden in the King's throne, making the King's courage the key to the party obtaining a legendary weapon.

The seventh shard of the Looking Glass has been in the Queen's crown all along — she shattered the mirror deliberately to prevent anyone from leaving Wonderland, and kept the most powerful shard as a source of additional power. The shard is also what allows her to detect lies (Truesight), making it both a weapon and a vulnerability (without it, she can be deceived).

The flamingo mallets on the croquet field are polymorphed courtiers who displeased the Queen. Freeing them not only liberates innocent people but provides the party with combat-capable noble allies for the final battle.

The Knave of Hearts did not steal the tarts — the Queen ate them herself and framed the Knave for refusing to laugh at her joke. This absurd injustice, when exposed publicly, becomes the catalyst for the card-soldiers' disillusionment with the Queen's regime.

The King of Hearts has been the real resistance leader all along — pardoning prisoners, hiding weapons, and quietly waiting for someone brave enough to give him a reason to act. His smaller throne literally conceals the weapon that can defeat the Queen.

The trial records beneath the judge's bench prove the Queen's claim to the throne is fraudulent — she seized power in a coup. If made public, this information turns even the most loyal card-soldiers against her, potentially eliminating the reinforcement problem in the final battle entirely.

The Looking Glass, once completed, does not merely create a gateway — it stabilizes Wonderland itself. The Queen's rule has been slowly destabilizing the realm, and the shattered mirror was both symptom and cause. Restoring it weakens the Queen's reality-warping powers significantly, making the final battle easier if the party completes the mirror before confronting her.
dmTips: This scenario is designed to be approached in multiple ways: full stealth (avoid all combat until the Looking Glass Chamber), full diplomacy (turn the court and army against the Queen without fighting her directly), full rebellion (inspire an uprising and storm the palace with an army), or full assault (fight through everything). All approaches are viable. The best sessions will see the party combining elements of all four based on their strengths and the opportunities they've created.

The Queen's Temper Gauge in the croquet match is the scenario's most important pacing tool. Track it openly and let the players see the consequences of their choices in real time. If the party is struggling, have the Cheshire Cat intervene with a distraction that lowers the gauge by 1. If the party is managing too easily, have the Queen notice something suspicious (the party whispering, a hedgehog cooperating too willingly) that raises it by 1.

The courtroom trial can run long — it is a complex social encounter with many moving parts. If it starts to drag, have the Queen lose patience and accelerate the proceedings: 'ENOUGH EVIDENCE! VERDICT!' This forces a climactic moment where the party must either accept the verdict, fight, or play their strongest card (the tart evidence, the court records, or direct challenge to the Queen's authority).

The mirror reflections in the Looking Glass Chamber are potentially the hardest combat in the scenario because they are literally the party's own stats turned against them. Balance this by encouraging the reconciliation option early — describe the reflections pausing momentarily, studying their originals with something that might be curiosity. If the party engages entirely through combat, consider reducing the reflections' HP to 75% of their originals to prevent a TPK.

The final battle with the Queen should feel genuinely dangerous but also triumphant. The arrival of the party's allies is the emotional payoff for the entire campaign — make it big. Describe each ally group arriving with their own moment: the card-painters bursting through a side door with paint pots raised like grenades, the Knave of Hearts cutting through card-soldiers with professional efficiency, the King of Hearts rising from his throne in slow motion. If the party broke the Tea Quarter's curse, the Hatter and March Hare's arrival should be the biggest cheer moment of the campaign.

The Crown of Hearts' corruption adds moral complexity to the Queen's defeat. If the party removes and destroys the crown, the Queen reverts to a confused, diminished fey who may not fully comprehend what she did. This creates interesting post-battle roleplay: do the card-soldiers demand justice? Does the King defend his wife? Does Wonderland forgive or punish? Let the party navigate this — there is no single correct answer.

Track which allies the party has earned throughout the campaign and have them appear in the final battle with mechanical effects: Card-painters provide distracting paint-pot attacks (card-soldiers hit by paint have disadvantage on attacks for 1 round). Freed flamingo-nobles engage card-soldier reinforcements, reducing the number that reach the Throne Room. The Knave of Hearts fights as a veteran alongside the party. The Hatter throws temporal disruption devices (as Slow spell on a single target). The March Hare engages one Vorpal Guard solo, keeping it occupied for 3 rounds. This makes each alliance feel mechanically meaningful, not just narratively satisfying.

The party's choice at the Looking Glass — escape or fight — should be genuinely agonizing. Do not telegraph which choice is 'correct.' Both are valid. If the party escapes, describe Wonderland growing small and distant through the glass, and the last thing they see is the Queen's furious face and the King's sad, accepting nod. If they fight, describe the weight of the decision: they are choosing to risk their lives for a world that is not theirs, for people made of cards and talking animals and sentient tea parties, and that choice is heroic precisely because it is unnecessary. Either way, honor the decision with narrative weight.

For groups that want an extended epilogue: after the Queen falls and the Looking Glass is restored, describe a 'Victory Tea Party' at the Hatter's table — now unfrozen, now real, now joyous. Every NPC the party helped attends. The Hatter makes a speech. The March Hare introduces his children. The Dormouse tells a story that is actually coherent. The card-painters paint a mural of the party's adventures. And when the party finally steps through the Looking Glass to go home, Wonderland waves goodbye — every rose, every card, every clock — and the last thing they hear before the mirror closes is the sound of a world, mad and impossible and beautiful, laughing with joy for the first time in centuries.
